issues.legal_issue: A successor who inherits a tenancy also inherits obligations incurred by the deceased tenant.
material_facts: The tenancy was inherited by the deceased tenant’s widow and minor son.
The landlord alleged that the deceased tenant had sublet the premises and that the arrangement continued after his death.
The courts below did not decide the subletting claim on its merits, relying on an earlier decision that treated a successor as not inheriting a predecessor’s rent-law breach.
issues.conclusion: The heirs inherited the obligations attached to the tenancy along with the tenancy rights; the contrary reasoning in the decisions below could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Tenancy is heritable unless a legal bar to heritability is shown. A successor takes the tenancy subject to the predecessor’s rights and obligations and cannot obtain a better tenancy right by inheritance. The Court relied on the three-Judge decision in Imdad Ali v. Keshav Chand, which rejected the general observations in A.S. Sulochana v. C. Dharmalingam to the extent that they suggested that a successor does not inherit the predecessor’s rent-law breach. The Court also noted that the relevant provision, Section 14(2)(ii)(a) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, permits eviction where the tenant, without the landlord’s written consent, transfers rights under the lease or sublets the premises.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.inherited_tenancy: A successor acquired the tenancy through inheritance from a deceased tenant.
predicates.predecessor_incurred_tenancy_obligation: The deceased tenant incurred an obligation arising from the tenancy before the successor inherited it.

issues.definition: When eviction is sought under rent-control law and a successor inherits a tenancy subject to an obligation incurred by the deceased tenant, the successor inherits that tenancy obligation.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s entry into a partnership with another person does not, by itself, establish that the tenant sublet the premises or parted with possession.
material_facts: The deceased tenant and another person had entered into a partnership concerning the business carried on at the premises.
After the tenant died, the tenant’s widow, acting for herself and the minor child, entered into another partnership with the other person.
The landlord alleged subletting, but the courts below had not assessed that allegation on its merits.
issues.conclusion: The existence of a partnership does not necessarily establish subletting or parting with possession. If the tenant remains actively associated with the business and retains use and control of the premises, the partnership alone may not amount to parting with possession; the real nature of the arrangement must be assessed where control or use has been transferred under cover of a partnership.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 14(2)(ii)(a) of the Himachal Pradesh Urban Rent Control Act, 1987, transferring rights under a lease or subletting without the landlord’s written consent may constitute a ground for eviction. A partnership may be genuine, with the tenant retaining use and control, or may disguise a transfer of possession or control for consideration. The court must examine the actual transaction rather than infer subletting merely from the partnership deed.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant under rent-control law on an allegation of subletting or transfer of tenancy rights.
predicates.tenant_entered_partnership: The tenant entered into a partnership with another person concerning business at the rented premises.
predicates.tenant_retained_use_and_control: The tenant remained actively associated with the business and retained use and control of the rented premises.

issues.definition: If a tenant enters a partnership but remains actively associated with the business and retains use and control of the premises, the partnership alone does not establish subletting.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord who is not a party to a partnership deed may adduce evidence to show that the deed conceals a transfer of possession or control of the rented premises.
material_facts: The landlord alleged that the partnership arrangements concealed an unlawful subletting or transfer of possession.
The landlord was a stranger to the partnership deeds.
The landlord sought a decision based on the evidence already adduced by the parties.
issues.conclusion: The partnership deed does not prevent the landlord from adducing evidence or using cross-examination to establish the real nature of the transaction, including that possession or control was transferred or that the deed was a cloak for an unlawful arrangement.
issues.legal_principle: The rule excluding oral evidence that varies or contradicts a written document governs the parties to that document; a stranger to it is not precluded from showing that it is untrue, collusive, or brought into existence for a fraudulent or illegal purpose. The Court relied on Tyagaraja v. Vedathanni, AIR 1936 PC 70, for the admissibility of oral evidence to show that a written deed did not record the real transaction.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks eviction under rent-control law based on an alleged transfer or subletting of rented premises.
predicates.landlord_is_stranger_to_partnership_deed: The landlord was not a party to the partnership deed relied on to describe the arrangement at the premises.
predicates.landlord_seeks_to_show_deed_conceals_tra: The landlord seeks to establish that the deed concealed a transfer of possession or control, or another transaction different from the one it recites.

issues.definition: When a landlord who was not a party to a partnership deed seeks to show that it concealed a transfer of possession or control, the landlord may prove the real transaction.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court must determine the merits of an eviction claim that was left undecided because the courts below relied on an incorrect legal rule.
material_facts: The landlord’s eviction claim included an allegation of subletting.
The Controller, the appellate authority, and the High Court did not decide the subletting claim on its merits because they relied on the rule in A.S. Sulochana.
The landlord submitted that the relevant evidence had been adduced and that the appellate authority could assess it.
The proceedings had already been pending for a substantial period.
issues.conclusion: The appeals were allowed, the decisions of the High Court and appellate authority were set aside, and the matter was remanded to the appellate authority to hear the parties and decide the appeal afresh, including whether a ground for eviction was established.
issues.legal_principle: Where the courts below have not examined an eviction ground on its merits because they applied an incorrect legal rule, and the relevant evidence is available for assessment, the appropriate course may be to set aside the decisions and remit the matter for fresh determination. The governing legal analysis includes the rule in Imdad Ali that successors inherit tenancy obligations and the factual inquiry into whether a partnership arrangement involved a transfer of possession or control.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_appeal: An appeal concerns a decision on a landlord’s application to evict a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.eviction_ground_not_decided_on_merits_du: The courts below left an eviction ground undecided on its merits because they relied on an incorrect legal rule.
predicates.evidence_available_for_appellate_assessm: The evidence needed to determine the eviction ground has been adduced and is available for assessment by the appellate authority.

issues.definition: When an eviction appeal concerns a ground left undecided on its merits because of an incorrect legal rule, and the evidence is available for appellate assessment, the matter is remanded for a fresh appellate decision.
